stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Immunologist Lena Okafor and colleagues found that adults who received a tuberculosis vaccine mounted stronger innate immune responses to several unrelated viruses three months later. Okafor concludes that the vaccine "trains" innate immune cells, giving recipients broad protection that reaches well beyond tuberculosis.

Text 2
Okafor's findings certainly offer encouraging evidence that innate immune cells can be trained. Still, when the same volunteers were retested, the heightened response had faded in most of them within a year. It's important to consider, then, that whatever broad protection the vaccine confers may be temporary.
choices: A tuberculosis vaccine can strengthen innate immune responses to pathogens other than tuberculosis.
The broad protection offered by a tuberculosis vaccine is likely to fade within a year.
Okafor's results offer little real evidence that innate immune cells can be trained.
The vaccine's effect on innate immune cells lasts long enough to protect recipients permanently.
explanation: Text 2 opens with a concession: Okafor's findings "certainly offer encouraging evidence" that innate cells can be trained. Then it turns on "Still" and adds a limit, which is that the effect may not last. Since Text 2 accepts the main finding, both authors agree that the vaccine strengthens innate responses to other pathogens. They differ only on how long that lasts.

B.why: You picked the caveat that only Text 2 raises. Okafor never says the protection fades, so you can't assume she would agree. A shared statement has to be something both authors accept.

C.why: You read "Still" as a full rejection. Text 2 says explicitly that the findings "certainly offer encouraging evidence." It limits Okafor's conclusion without dismissing it.

D.why: Okafor claims broad protection, not permanent protection, so this is a stronger version of her view than she gives. Text 2 also suggests the effect may be temporary, so neither author supports this.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After Halverton added protected bike lanes to its downtown streets, urban planner Rafael Duarte recorded a 40 percent rise in cycling trips there within two years. Duarte concludes that physically separating cyclists from traffic draws new riders and that other cities should follow Halverton's lead.

Text 2
Duarte's figures deserve attention, and the downtown lanes clearly mattered. But Halverton also built protected lanes in its outlying neighborhoods during the same period, and cycling there barely changed. Where trips run long, separation from traffic may matter less than distance itself.
choices: Protected bike lanes are unlikely to raise cycling in neighborhoods where trips are long.
The rise in downtown cycling was probably caused by something other than the lanes.
Protected bike lanes contributed to the increase in cycling in downtown Halverton.
Protected bike lanes raise cycling by roughly the same amount in every part of a city.
explanation: Text 2 grants that "the downtown lanes clearly mattered," then pivots on "But" to a case where they didn't help much: the outlying neighborhoods. This narrows Duarte's claim without overturning it. Both authors therefore agree that the lanes helped raise cycling downtown.

A.why: This is the limit that only Text 2 adds. Duarte says nothing about outlying neighborhoods, and his call for other cities to copy Halverton suggests he would not accept it.

B.why: You treated the "But" as full disagreement. Text 2 explicitly says the downtown lanes "clearly mattered," so its author does not credit the rise to some other cause.

D.why: Duarte never claims equal effects everywhere, so this is a stronger version of his view than he gives. Text 2's outlying-neighborhood data also show the effect was not equal.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Before the 1850s, vivid purples and magentas came from costly natural sources and were worn largely by the wealthy. Historian Miriam Castell argues that cheap synthetic aniline dyes, introduced late in that decade, changed this, bringing brightly colored clothing within reach of working-class households.

Text 2
Castell has shown convincingly that aniline dyes put bright fabrics within reach of working families in industrial towns. It's important to consider, however, that many rural weavers, who dyed their own cloth, kept using plant dyes for decades, so the change she describes unfolded far more slowly in the countryside.
choices: Rural weavers continued to rely on plant dyes long after aniline dyes were introduced.
Synthetic dyes made brightly colored clothing affordable for at least some working-class people.
Aniline dyes did little to change who could afford to wear brightly colored clothing.
Aniline dyes replaced plant dyes in towns and villages alike within a few years.
explanation: Text 2 begins by crediting Castell ("has shown convincingly"). It then turns on "It's important to consider, however" to say the change came more slowly in rural areas. Because Text 2 accepts that aniline dyes reached working families in towns, both authors agree that synthetic dyes made bright clothing affordable for at least some working-class people.

A.why: This is Text 2's added limit. Castell doesn't discuss rural weavers, so the texts give you no reason to think she would agree.

C.why: You took the caveat as a rejection. Text 2 says Castell has "shown convincingly" that the dyes reached working families. It disputes only how quickly the change spread.

D.why: Castell never claims a fast, complete replacement everywhere, so this is a stronger claim than Text 1 makes. Text 2 directly denies it for the countryside.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a five-year trial on rain-fed farms in the U.S. Midwest, agronomist Priya Natarajan found that fields sown with cereal rye between corn harvests gained soil organic matter and produced higher corn yields than fields left bare. She therefore recommends cover crops to grain farmers generally.

Text 2
Natarajan's trial certainly offers encouraging insight into what cover crops can do for soil. But in semiarid regions, a rye crop growing through spring draws down moisture the following crop needs, and yields there have sometimes fallen. Her recommendation may hold only where rainfall is reliable.
choices: Cover crops tend to lower corn yields in regions with little spring rainfall.
Natarajan's trial reveals little about how cover crops affect soil.
Cover crops will raise grain yields on farms regardless of local rainfall.
Cover crops can benefit soil on farms that receive reliable rainfall.
explanation: Text 2 concedes that the trial "certainly offers encouraging insight" into how cover crops help soil. After "But," it limits where the recommendation applies: places with reliable rainfall. Natarajan's trial took place on rain-fed Midwest farms and showed soil gains, so both authors agree that cover crops can benefit soil where rainfall is reliable.

A.why: Only Text 2 raises the problem in dry regions. Natarajan doesn't address semiarid farms, and her general recommendation suggests she wouldn't accept this claim.

B.why: You treated the "But" as a dismissal. Text 2 explicitly credits the trial with "encouraging insight" into soil effects.

C.why: You ignored the caveat. Natarajan's broad recommendation might fit this claim, but Text 2 rejects it, saying yields have fallen where rainfall is scarce.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Ornithologist Tomas Lindqvist tracked banded black-capped chickadees through three winters and found that birds with access to backyard feeders survived at markedly higher rates than birds without it. He argues that feeding stations provide a meaningful lifeline for small songbirds during the coldest months.

Text 2
Lindqvist's survival data are hard to argue with: feeders plainly help chickadees through winter. Still, feeders also crowd birds together at a single point, and outbreaks of contagious eye disease among house finches have been traced to unclean feeders. Any accounting of their value has to include that cost.
choices: Feeders contribute to the spread of contagious disease among house finches.
Lindqvist's data fail to show that feeders benefit chickadees in winter.
Backyard feeders can improve the winter survival of black-capped chickadees.
Feeding stations benefit every visiting bird species without any notable drawback.
explanation: Text 2 concedes that the data are "hard to argue with" and that feeders "plainly help chickadees through winter." After "Still," it adds a cost that Text 1 left out, which is the spread of disease. The concession is the shared ground: both authors agree that feeders improve chickadees' winter survival.

A.why: This is the cost that only Text 2 adds. Lindqvist never mentions disease or house finches, so you can't attribute this view to him.

B.why: You read "Still" as full disagreement. Text 2 says outright that feeders "plainly help chickadees," so it accepts Lindqvist's finding.

D.why: Lindqvist studied only chickadees and never claims there are no drawbacks, so this is a stronger version of his view. Text 2 names a drawback directly.

stimulus:
Text 1
Volunteer mapping platforms let anyone trace roads and buildings from satellite imagery. When geographer Ana Ruiz compared volunteer maps of rural road networks in northern Peru with a government field survey, she found the two nearly identical. Ruiz concludes that volunteer mapping can reliably fill gaps in rural maps.

Text 2
Ruiz's comparison deserved the attention it received; volunteers clearly trace roads well. But much of what rural residents need on a map, such as footpaths under tree cover, field boundaries, and local place names, cannot be seen from above. For those features, remote volunteers remain a poor substitute for local knowledge.
choices: Volunteers working from satellite imagery can map rural roads accurately.
Volunteer maps tend to leave out footpaths, field boundaries, and place names.
Volunteer maps of rural areas are too unreliable to be of practical use.
Volunteer maps capture every rural feature as well as a field survey does.
explanation: Text 2 credits Ruiz's comparison and grants that "volunteers clearly trace roads well." It then pivots on "But" to features that can't be seen from above. That narrows Ruiz's conclusion without denying her finding. Both authors agree that volunteers can map rural roads accurately.

B.why: Only Text 2 makes this point. Ruiz compared road networks alone and says nothing about footpaths or place names, so you can't assume she agrees.

C.why: You treated the "But" as a dismissal. Text 2 concedes that volunteers map roads well and doubts them only for certain features.

D.why: Ruiz tested only roads, so this is a stronger claim than Text 1 makes. Text 2 explicitly lists features that volunteers miss.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
During a magnitude 6.4 earthquake last year, a regional early-warning system sent alerts to phones in Valmora 15 seconds before strong shaking arrived, enough time for trains to brake and students to take cover. Seismologist Hana Moreau concludes that such systems give the public meaningful protection.

Text 2
Moreau is right that alerts can buy precious seconds, as they did in Valmora, about 90 kilometers from the epicenter. But the system needs several seconds to detect a quake and issue a warning, so people closest to the source often feel shaking before any alert arrives. Protection shrinks precisely where shaking is strongest.
choices: People near an earthquake's source often receive alerts too late to help.
Alerts usually arrive too late to be of any practical use to the public.
Every resident in a quake zone will receive at least 15 seconds of warning.
Early-warning alerts can give some people time to take protective action before shaking.
explanation: Text 2 opens with "Moreau is right that alerts can buy precious seconds." After "But," it adds a case where the claim doesn't hold: people near the epicenter. The concession is the shared ground, so both authors agree that alerts can give some people time to protect themselves.

A.why: This is the limit that only Text 2 introduces. Moreau doesn't discuss people near the epicenter, so the texts don't show that she would agree.

B.why: You read the "But" as full rejection. Text 2 says Moreau "is right" that alerts can buy precious seconds, as they did in Valmora.

C.why: Moreau reports 15 seconds for one city. She never promises that to every resident, so this is a stronger version of her claim. Text 2 also says some people get no warning in time.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Recordings made between 1900 and 1920 capture violinists sliding audibly between notes and stretching tempos in ways later players rarely did. Musicologist Daniel Achebe argues that these discs preserve precisely how musicians of that era performed, making them a more trustworthy guide than written treatises.

Text 2
Achebe rightly treats early recordings as indispensable evidence of period style. Yet a disc side then held only about four minutes of music, and players often rushed or trimmed pieces to fit. The slides may be faithful, but the tempos are another matter.
choices: Performers on early discs often played faster than they would have in concert.
Early recordings are valuable evidence of how musicians around 1900 performed.
Early recordings reveal little about the performing style of that period.
The tempos on early recordings match those the musicians used in concert.
explanation: Text 2 concedes that Achebe "rightly treats early recordings as indispensable evidence." It then turns on "Yet" to a missing factor: the short disc side, which distorted tempos. Since Text 2 keeps Achebe's main point, both authors agree that early recordings are valuable evidence of period performance.

A.why: This is the caveat that only Text 2 raises. Achebe says the recordings preserve performance "precisely," so he would not accept that the tempos were rushed.

C.why: You treated "Yet" as full disagreement. Text 2 calls the recordings "indispensable evidence" and even accepts that the slides may be faithful.

D.why: You went with pure agreement and ignored the caveat. Achebe might accept this, but Text 2 rejects it outright: "the tempos are another matter."
